passage.title: The Restorative Work of the Sleeping Brain

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, science treated sleep as little more than a nightly switch-off. That view has been abandoned. Contemporary neuroscience describes sleep as an active, staged process in which the brain replays recent experience, prunes redundant connections and clears metabolic waste, and the quality of this work is now recognised as a major determinant of memory, learning and everyday judgement. The stakes are considerable: survey data for 2026 suggest that a large fraction of adults in industrialised countries falls short of the recommended seven to nine hours.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, and above all in its deepest slow-wave phase, the hippocampus appears to orchestrate the transfer of freshly acquired information to the neocortex for long-term storage. The process is driven by sharp-wave ripples, brief high-frequency bursts during which the day's neural firing patterns are replayed at compressed speed. Sleep spindles, short oscillations generated by the thalamus, are thought to coordinate this dialogue between the two regions. The strength of coupling between slow oscillations, spindles and ripples predicts overnight memory gains more reliably than total sleep time alone.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, by contrast, has come to be seen less as a recording device and more as an editing suite. Research has identified neurons in the hypothalamus, active almost exclusively during REM, that project to the hippocampus and appear to weaken or erase selected memories, contrary to the popular assumption that dreaming strengthens everything. A 2026 eLife study by Justin Shin of Brandeis University described patterns of cortical-hippocampal reactivation during REM, driven by chains of high-frequency oscillations in the prefrontal cortex, that differ fundamentally from those of NREM sleep. This editing function may explain why the emotional charge of a painful experience fades across successive nights of dreaming.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The cognitive cost of lost sleep is cumulative and easy to underestimate. In a landmark experiment at the University of Pennsylvania, Hans Van Dongen and colleagues restricted volunteers to six hours of sleep per night for two weeks; by the end, their performance on attention and working-memory tasks had fallen to a level equivalent to two nights of total sleep deprivation, yet the participants reported feeling only mildly sleepy. The gap between subjective tiredness and objective impairment is one of the most consistent findings in the field. A 2026 study in Advanced Science by Ke Zhou's group at Beijing Normal University offers a physiological explanation: 36 hours of wakefulness pushes large-scale brain dynamics from a near-critical state towards a supercritical one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Prevalence data gathered in 2026 confirm that short sleep is no longer confined to a small minority. The Sleep Health Foundation's Aussie Sleep Snapshot Survey found that more than half of Australians (54.2 per cent) reported sleeping poorly three or more nights a week, and that 36.9 per cent of workers attributed poor nights to work-related factors, with the figure rising above 46 per cent among those aged 25-34. In China, a white paper released by the China Sleep Research Association in 2026 put the rate of sleep disturbance among adults at 48.5 per cent. Across industrialised countries, adolescents fare no better; most teenagers sleep less than the eight to ten hours recommended for their age.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: School start times have become a focus of research. During adolescence the biological clock shifts later, so that teenagers feel sleepy at a later hour than adults, making early first bells a structural cause of chronic sleep restriction. A 2026 study from the University of Zurich examined a Swiss secondary school that introduced flexible start times, allowing students to arrive between 7.30 and 8.30. Ninety-five per cent of the pupils chose the later option, gained roughly 45 minutes of sleep a night, and reported better sleep quality and well-being, with improved results in English and mathematics. An analysis of California's Senate Bill 328, the first statewide mandate of later starts, found that the share of adolescents sleeping at least eight hours rose by 13 percentage points, with measurable gains in eighth-grade test scores.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Evening exposure to the short-wavelength light emitted by screens is frequently blamed for disrupting sleep, because such light suppresses the production of melatonin. The evidence, however, is more nuanced than much popular advice suggests. A meta-analysis published in JAMA Pediatrics in 2026, pooling 25 studies of 4,562 young people, compared each individual's high-screen days with their own low-screen days and found that screens were associated with a later bedtime but showed no significant link to total sleep time, sleep efficiency or sleep quality. The one exception was screen use after getting into bed. Researchers concluded that the cognitive and emotional arousal generated by content may interfere with sleep more than the light itself.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Employers have begun to treat sleep as a productivity issue. The RAND Corporation has estimated the economic cost of sleep deprivation in the United States at more than US$400 billion a year in lost productivity, and a 2026 report from WebMD Health Services found that 69 per cent of employees sleep fewer than seven hours a night. Yet optimism about repair must be tempered. While a single recovery night reverses many acute deficits, chronic sleep debt appears to require days or weeks of regular sleep to clear, and some long-term changes may not be fully reversible. The balance of evidence suggests that consistent, adequate sleep, rather than weekend catch-up, is the foundation of both memory and cognitive performance.

question_groups.instruction: The reading passage has eight paragraphs, A-H. Choose the correct heading for paragraphs A, C, D, G and H from the list of headings below.

options.text: Sleep as an active biological process rather than a passive nightly rest
The mechanism by which slow-wave sleep transfers memories to long-term storage
Dreaming may weaken memories as well as strengthening them
Sleep loss accumulates gradually while the sleeper remains unaware
Why flexible school schedules benefit adolescent sleep and results
The association between late bedtimes and falling academic results
A challenge to the assumption that screens are the main cause of poor sleep
The financial case for employer-led sleep programmes
The limited capacity of the body to repay accumulated sleep loss

evidence.quote: Contemporary neuroscience describes sleep as an active, staged process in which the brain replays recent experience

paraphrase.from: an active biological process rather than a passive nightly rest
paraphrase.to: sleep as an active, staged process in which the brain replays recent experience

questions.explanation: A 段开篇即抛弃"睡眠是被动休息"的旧观点，主张睡眠是主动、分阶段的过程，对应标题 i。

evidence.quote: neurons in the hypothalamus, active almost exclusively during REM, that project to the hippocampus and appear to weaken or erase selected memories

paraphrase.from: Dreaming may weaken memories as well as strengthening them
paraphrase.to: neurons in the hypothalamus ... appear to weaken or erase selected memories

questions.explanation: C 段核心是说 REM 睡眠中的下丘脑神经元会弱化或清除部分记忆，即做梦既能强化也能削弱记忆，对应标题 iii。

evidence.quote: their performance on attention and working-memory tasks had fallen to a level equivalent to two nights of total sleep deprivation, yet the participants reported feeling only mildly sleepy

paraphrase.from: Sleep loss accumulates gradually while the sleeper remains unaware
paraphrase.to: the cognitive cost of lost sleep is cumulative ... yet the participants reported feeling only mildly sleepy

questions.explanation: D 段强调睡眠不足的损伤是累积的，且本人往往察觉不到，对应标题 iv。

evidence.quote: screens were associated with a later bedtime but showed no significant link to total sleep time, sleep efficiency or sleep quality

paraphrase.from: A challenge to the assumption that screens are the main cause of poor sleep
paraphrase.to: screens were associated with a later bedtime but showed no significant link to total sleep time

questions.explanation: G 段用 2026 年荟萃分析说明屏幕主要推迟就寝时间、与睡眠质量无显著关联，质疑"屏幕是睡眠不良主因"的常见说法，对应标题 vii。

evidence.quote: The RAND Corporation has estimated the economic cost of sleep deprivation in the United States at more than US$400 billion a year in lost productivity

paraphrase.from: The financial case for employer-led sleep programmes
paraphrase.to: employers have begun to treat sleep as a productivity issue

questions.explanation: H 段先以 RAND 的经济成本估算引出雇主把睡眠当作生产力议题，对应标题 viii。
